implementation_notes: Swift's standard library does not ship atomic types; the swift-atomics package (Apple's) provides Atomic, ManagedAtomic and the ordering types, which wrap the C11 primitives on Apple platforms and LLVM's IR atomics elsewhere. Ordering is explicit - .relaxed, .acquiring, .releasing, .acquiringAndReleasing - which is the right level of control and the same set as C11. Since Swift 6, strict concurrency checking makes the safety requirements compiler-enforced: a non-Sendable type cannot cross an isolation boundary, which eliminates a whole class of the bug this pattern's tradeoffs describe. os_unfair_lock and OSAllocatedUnfairLock are the pragmatic alternative when you do not need non-blocking progress.
pitfalls: swift-atomics is a package dependency, not the standard library - a project that forgets it has no atomic type at all.
A ManagedAtomic is a class with a deinitialiser, so it allocates; use Atomic<T> for value types where Swift's exclusivity permits.
Ordering choices are not checked for correctness - .relaxed on a store that publishes data compiles fine and fails on ARM.
Mutex.lock() from Foundation is not the same as os_unfair_lock and has different priority-inversion behaviour; use the OS primitive where latency matters.
alternative: OSAllocatedUnfairLock or actors when you need mutual exclusion rather than a non-blocking atomic; an actor when you need serialised access to several fields
